description: We are building a browser game for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Kids aged 7–12 run a lunar outpost near the Moon’s south pole and make real trade-offs between power, life support, radiation shielding and food, using NASA data like DONKI solar storms, LOLA terrain and Blue Marble imagery. Skills: frontend, backend, Python, 3D web (three.js) and research. We’d love a 3D artist or animator, a sound designer, and a teacher to playtest with kids.
summary:
Lunar Outpost is a  browser-based 3D game that trains kids aged 7–12 to think like astronauts. Players create their own astronaut, walk through a launch centre, ride the countdown to liftoff, launch to the Moon and run a lunar outpost with a crew of four.

Along the way, crew members ask the player for help with 12 real mission problems: fixing a CO2 scrubber, choosing a power source, picking a landing site, rationing water and food, driving a rover before its battery runs out, and sheltering from solar storms. Each choice is a trade-off between resources, crew health and radiation dose, and those choices lead to one of four endings.

The game is built on real NASA data. Moon terrain comes from LRO's LOLA elevation maps, solar storms come from NASA's DONKI space-weather records, and radiation limits and Earth–Moon radio delay come from NASA studies. A kid-friendly Mission Handbook then explains what happened, what a better choice would have been, and how it connects to real missions like Artemis.

It runs in any web browser, needs no install, and works on school laptops with basic graphics.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Outpost is a 3D browser game for kids aged 7–12. The player creates their own astronaut and plays one continuous mission in three parts:

1. Earth – explore the launch centre, meet the crew, take the elevator and tunnel out to the rocket, and ride the countdown to liftoff, with cinematic cutscenes for launch and booster separation.

2. Space – live aboard the spacecraft in realistic zero-gravity (push off and glide), solve problems with the crew, and land on the Moon.

3. Lunar outpost – run the base near the lunar south pole: manage power, water, food and air, drive a rover across real Moon terrain, and protect the crew from solar storms and meteoroids.

HOW IT WORKS

Instead of reading lessons, kids are asked for help. A crewmate says, for example, "Hey Rishab, I'm having trouble figuring this out , can you help me decide?" and the player takes over a decision panel. There are 12 challenges: CO2 scrubber repair, power source, landing site, water ice, food, rover range, radiation shelter and more. Every option is a trade-off: there is never a "free" choice, and the game checks this automatically. Choices change three meters (resources, crew health and radiation dose) and come back later in the story, leading to one of four endings.

Random hazards (solar storms in transit and on the Moon, meteoroid hits on solar panels) are rolled each game, up to three of each, so no two missions are the same. At the end, a picture-book Mission Handbook shows the mission day by day: what each choice did, what a better choice would have been, how much was skill and how much was luck, and how it connects to real NASA missions. A guidebook (G key) gives a kid-friendly glossary, a table of where every task is, and the controls.

REAL NASA DATA

• Moon terrain is built from LRO LOLA south-pole elevation data, and the Moon and Earth use NASA SVS imagery (LROC, Blue Marble).

• Solar storms come from NASA's DONKI space-weather database. Storm frequency is scaled from real recorded events, and the game can show live space weather.

• Radiation is shown in millisieverts against NASA dose limits, and Earth–Moon radio delay comes from a NASA technical report.

• Science facts in the Handbook link to NASA OSDR space biology studies.

Every number in the game is listed with its source in the repository. Numbers we could not source are marked rather than invented.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Kids practise what real mission planners do: weighing trade-offs, managing limited resources, thinking about safety and learning from mistakes. Because the crew asks for help and reacts to the player's choices, kids feel responsible for real people, not just a score. The Handbook turns every ending, including a bad one, into a lesson, and encourages replaying with better choices. Our goal is for a 7-year-old to finish a mission understanding why astronauts care about air, water, power and radiation, and to feel that they could be part of the next Moon crew.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

• One continuous story from Earth to the Moon, with cutscenes, a voiced crew with expressive talking portraits, and radio and hologram messages from Houston.

• Choices that are remembered and come back later in the mission.

• A "luck vs skill" verdict, so kids learn that good decisions still face risk.

• A friendship story: your best friend since primary school is on the crew.

• A crew named in honour of real astronaut pioneers from many countries.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

• Age: short sentences, big text, pictures for every word, a readability check, and pop-up guides.

• Accuracy: no invented NASA numbers, and realistic zero-g movement and launch sequence.

• Access: runs in a normal web browser with no install or login, and is tuned to run on a basic school laptop with integrated graphics and 8 GB RAM.

• Honesty about AI: AI-generated voices and AI-assisted code are credited in the game and the repository.

• Licences: every third-party model, texture and font is credited in ASSETS.md.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

TypeScript, React 19, three.js, React Three Fiber and drei, zustand, and Vite. A static website with no backend. Node scripts fetch and process NASA data (LOLA, DONKI) and build textures. Automated checks run on every build. CC0 textures come from ambientCG and Poly Haven. Crew voices were made with ElevenLabs. Developed on a Linux laptop (Intel i7-1165G7 with Iris Xe graphics).
dataRefs: LRO LOLA South Pole Elevation Model (LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ, Barker et al. 2023) – game terrain
NASA DONKI Space Weather Database – solar flares and storms
NASA Open APIs (DONKI API) – live space weather
NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LRO LROC imagery) – Moon textures
NASA SVS Blue Marble – Earth imagery
NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) – space biology studies
NASA-STD-3001 Radiation Protection Technical Brief – 600 mSv career and 250 mSv solar-event dose limits
NASA Technical Memorandum NASA/TM-20250003885 – Earth–Moon communication delay
